_comment: Weights for the deterministic keyword prescore in fetch_jobs.py.
This is a keyword match, not a judgment. It exists so the pipeline works with
no model in the loop, and so that when the agent does score a posting you have
something transparent to compare it against.
Points are additive. Title family and location take the single best match, in
ARRAY ORDER, because fetch_jobs.py breaks on the first hit. So a more specific
title must sit above a more general one, and the order of those two lists is
part of the logic rather than presentation. Keywords and penalties all apply.
The total is clamped to 0 to 100.
Matching is NEGATION AWARE, via mentions() in fetch_jobs.py. It has to be: a
genuine adoption-flavour deployment posting says 'no coding screen' precisely to
distinguish itself, and blind substring matching took the full coding-screen
penalty for saying so, ranking the trap above the role we want most.
Point values MATCH prompts/scoring-rubric.md exactly. Keep them in step. They
drifted once, 12/3/5 here against 15/8/0 there, with both files claiming to
encode the same scale.
Title families mirror the tiers in prompts/profile.md. They did not: an AI
product title scored 42, above every Tier 1 family, which inverted the ranking
the profile says to respect.
Penalties are scanned against title, description AND location. The out-of-scope
penalty is written entirely in place names, so scanning only title and
description let a London posting through with no penalty at all.
Every penalty here is a backstop. The real filters are in step 0 of
prompts/scoring-rubric.md, and three of them this prescore cannot see at all:
it cannot read a start date, it cannot judge whether a company has a New York
office, and it cannot weigh a requirements section. That is what the agent is
for, and it is why every rationale this script writes says so.
Ceiling check: title 45 plus location 15 plus every keyword is above 100, so the
clamp is reachable on paper but not in practice, because the keyword groups are
mutually unlikely. A real Tier 1 posting hits three or four and lands in the
eighties. If a run puts many rows at exactly 100, the clamp has started doing
the scoring and the weights need cutting.

title_families.label: Tier 1 deployment or applied AI lead title
title_families._note: Order is load-bearing: fetch_jobs.py breaks on the first match, so a more specific title must appear above a more general one. 'forward deployed' sits here because the title is genuinely ambiguous; the coding-screen penalty and the agent's requirements check are what separate the engineering flavour.

title_families.label: Tier 1 technical account management or enterprise customer success title
title_families._note: Must precede the adjacent-commercial family, which holds the generic 'account manager'. It did not, so 'technical account manager' was dead code: the generic pattern matched first and scored it 32.

title_families.label: post-sales, enablement or internal product ownership, no tier
title_families._note: Her old job rather than a target. See the 30 band in prompts/scoring-rubric.md.

title_families.label: Tier 2 go-to-market, partnerships or product marketing title
title_families._note: GTM is a target she asked for, not a title she has held. See the cap in prompts/scoring-rubric.md, which this prescore cannot apply.

title_families.label: Tier 3 product or analyst title
title_families._note: Growth PM ranks above generic AI PM for her, but a keyword matcher cannot see the difference, so the whole tier shares one band. Was 42 for an AI product title, which put Tier 3 above every Tier 1 family and inverted the ranking in profile.md.

keywords.label: enterprise or strategic accounts, post-sales ownership
keywords._note: One of the real positive signals. The word AI in a title is noise; this is not.

keywords.label: AI or model platform
keywords._note: Cut from 6. The word AI carries close to no signal now, so these patterns are worth a little as company-shape evidence and nothing more. What separates a real fit from a title match is the work described: enterprise accounts, post-sales, adoption, non-technical end users.

keywords.label: data quality and validation
keywords._note: Dropped bare 'ingest' and 'schema': they fired on prose like 'we ingest customer feedback into our schema of record'.

keywords.label: retail or consumer goods domain
keywords._note: Dropped bare 'retail' and 'e-commerce': they fired on 'healthcare and retail' listed as a customer vertical, which says nothing about the role.

keywords.label: part-time or student-compatible
keywords._note: Dropped bare 'contract': it fired on 'after the contract is signed', which is sales prose, not an employment term.

locations.label: New York
locations._note: Point values now match prompts/scoring-rubric.md exactly. They did not: this file had 12/3/5 where the rubric had 15/8/0, and both claimed to encode the same scale.

locations.label: another US metro, relationship only, not actionable
locations._note: Includes San Francisco. No comma-state patterns here: ', ca' also matched 'Toronto, Canada' and 'Remote, Canada', so a non-US row collected US location points on its way to the out-of-scope penalty. Spell the cities out instead.

penalties.label: outside the United States, out of scope
requires security clearance
penalties._note: Citizenship patterns moved to the authorization penalty. 'must be a us citizen' sat here at -30, so a posting the rubric says to DROP scored 38 and was written to out/candidates.json.

penalties.label: coding screen, so this is the engineering flavour
penalties._note: The disambiguation that matters. Forward deployed and AI deployment cover two different jobs under near-identical titles, and some manager-titled deployment roles smuggle in a coding screen. A keyword hit cannot read a requirements section, so this is a backstop: the real rule is in prompts/scoring-rubric.md step 0b, which tells the agent to classify on the requirements and drop the engineering version entirely.

penalties.label: hard product manager title screen
penalties._note: She has no PM title on record, so a hard years-as-a-PM screen makes the role low-probability whatever the fit. Deprioritise, do not drop: the agent caps it and flags the screen risk in the rationale.

penalties.label: requires existing US work authorization with no CPT or OPT accommodation
penalties._note: F-1. See the hard constraints in prompts/profile.md. The agent drops these outright; the prescore can only push them down. Raised to -60 and given the citizenship patterns: these are step 0 drops in prompts/scoring-rubric.md, so the prescore must push them to 0 rather than leave them scoring in the thirties.
patterns: must have permanent us work authorization
must be authorized to work in the united states without sponsorship
